To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1. IL-23/22 signaling regulates the relative abundance of specific commensal microbes, 2. IL-23R deficiency results in increased systemic dissemination of SFB, 3.
the IL-22/IL-23 pathway dynamically and selectively regulates commensal microbiome composition, and this in turn controls systemic dissemination of commensals and the magnitude of TH17 responses.

IL23R signaling in intestinal epithelial cells is essential to maintain barrier function and to control systemic dissemination of commensal microbes, which in turn limits the development of Th17 responses in distantly localized tissues.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of the immune system and the role that the intestinal microbiota plays in this regulation.
the regulation of the immune system by commensal bacteria and the consequences of this regulation for the development of inflammatory diseases.
the role of IL-23/ IL-22 in maintaining mucosal homeostasis and the role of commensal microbes therein.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
“The IL-23/ IL-22 axis is of critical importance in the maintenance of mucocutaneous barrier function and the control of commensal microbes.
IL23/IL22 signaling is of critical importance to normal immune homeostatic function through maintenance of mucosal barriers and containment of commensals.
IL23R signaling is critical in limiting the expansion of Th17 cells through the IL22-mediated containment and regulation of commensal bacteria.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
IL-23R signaling limits TH17 responses by containing the commensal microbiome through IL-22-mediated maintenance of the mucosal barrier.

the IL-22/IL-23 pathway is of critical for the maintenance of mucosa-associated commensals, and that this pathway is important for the maintenance of homeostatic immune responses in the absence of infection or overt inflammation.

the IL23R/IL22R axis plays a key role in maintaining immune homeostasis by regulating the relative abundance of commensal organisms in the intestine, which in turn limits TH17 responses in peripheral tissues.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the intestinal barrier is maintained by a dynamic balance between commensal organisms and the host immune system.
the IL-22/IL-23 pathway is of critical relevance for maintaining immune homeostasis.
a delicate balance exists between the immune system and the commensal microbiome.
